newsitem.title: UK: British Labour Party's row with unions deepens.
newsitem.headline: British Labour Party's row with unions deepens.

text.p: A bitter row between Britain's opposition Labour Party and its traditional trade union allies has deepened with demands by some union bosses for the dismissal of the party's employment spokesman Stephen Byers.

Byers, a close ally of party leader Tony Blair, was the source of newspaper reports on Thursday suggesting Labour could jettison its historic ties with the unions after the next general election. He says he was misreported.

Labour, which was formed by trade unionists at the end of the last century as their parliamentary voice, looks set to win the election, which must be held by next May, and to return to power for the first time since 1979.
Most opinion polls give it a lead of more than 20 points over the ruling Conservatives following Blair's rejection of many traditional socialist policies.
Some union leaders, convinced Byers did suggest the possibility of a divorce to reporters, on Saturday cast aside their reticence to criticise Labour ahead of the election.
"Stephen Byers should be sacked immediately," Kenneth Cameron, leader of the Firemen's Union, wrote in the tabloid Sun newspaper.
"How he can continue to talk to trade unionists as employment spokesman I don't know," John Edmonds, general secretary of the huge blue-collar GMB union, told independent television.
But newspapers on Saturday quoted aides to Blair as saying there was no question of Byers being sacked.
The trade unions supply over half Labour's cash, have half the votes at its annual conference and 12 members on its powerful 29-strong National Executive Committee.

Over a dinner in Blackpool, the northern seaside resort where the Trades Union Congress has been meeting this week, Byers chatted to four leading political journalists about the future of the relationship.
Their newspapers then carried similar reports suggesting that there was talk in Labour leadership circles about abandoning the traditional links.
"I am very disappointed...about the way my comments were misinterpreted by a number of newspapers today," Byers said.

But the journalists insisted their stories, in which Byers was not mentioned by name, were accurate. "The conversation cannot be detailed...but I stand by everything in that report," Jill Sherman of the Times wrote in Saturday's paper.

Cameron said in some unions, such as the railwaymen's RMT, there were already widespread calls for Labour ties to be cut, and for links to be forged with the new Socialist Labour Party set up by fiery miners' leader Arthur Scargill.
"So far Labour loyalists within the union have been able to resist that step. Statements like this will make their job much harder," he wrote.
But TUC general secretary John Monks said he had received an assurance from Blair that no consideration was being given to ending ties. "I have accepted this assurance," he said.
